senses: An aide-de-camp.
A racehorse.
A carousel or roundabout (especially in the plural)
The Chinamanfish, a type of snapper
examples: Lieutenant Coghill had been told to act as galloper to Colonel Glyn on the unfortunate reconnaissance made from Isandlwana Camp, on January 22, 1879
The Hussler's trainer, Ross McDonald, is confident Australia's champion galloper will win the clashes, despite Weekend Hussler never having competed over 1000m before.

senses: Flour made from a mixture of ground pulses and cereals.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi सत्तू (sattū), from Sanskrit सक्तु (saktu).

senses: A traditional Spanish unit of dry measure, equivalent to about 222 liters.
ety: From Spanish carga (“a load, 4 Spanish bushels”), from cargar (“to load”), from Late Latin carricāre, from Latin carrus (“cart”). Doublet of charge and cargo.

senses: A thick, creamy soup made from potato, leeks, onions, and chicken stock, and normally served cold.
Synonym of ferrous, of or related to iron.
Synonym of rusty, of or related to rust, rust-colored.
ety: Borrowed from Latin ferrūgineus, from ferrūgo (“rust”).

senses: One who kills deer.
examples: He’d enjoyed the rush of peering in a window at the deerslayers, but invariably they’d just been smoking like chimneys, drinking to excess, overeating, and acting like yahoos.

senses: One who betters, makes something better.
An early electronic keyboard instrument that played back prerecorded sounds.
ety: Brand name, possibly based on melo- + -tron.

senses: A preparation of crushed areca nut, tobacco, catechu, paraffin, slaked lime and sweet or savoury flavourings, chewed recreationally in India.
Meat slow-cooked over an open fire, characteristic of Latin American cuisine.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish barbacoa (whence also barbecue), from Taíno barbakoa (“framework of sticks”), the raised wooden structure the natives used to either sleep on or cure meat. Originally “meal of roasted meat or fish”. Doublet of barbecue and balbacua.

senses: A highly detailed, usually large-scale painting of a cityscape or some other vista.
ety: From Italian veduta. Doublet of view.

senses: Someone who ruins.
examples: There was a ruined uncle in the family group—ruined by his brother, the Father of the Marshalsea, and knowing no more how than his ruiner did, but accepting the fact as something that could not be helped.

senses: A type of traditional Korean house first designed and built in the 14th century during the Joseon Dynasty.
A process for utilising metal plates in a manner similar to lithographic stones.
A process of imitating the grain of wood on metals.
Having plumage.
examples: From my vantage point in one of four bleacher sections, the dancers tearing across the larger stage in the distance evoked images of brightly plumaged birds.

senses: Any of several other plants in the family Plantaginaceae.
Wearing a robe.
A study of the individuals in a group of people within a specific context and their relationships.
ety: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms: prosopo- + -graphy; from the Latin prosōpographia (“description of a person’s appearance; description of an individual’s life”), from the Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face, person”) + -γρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (-grăphĭ́ā, “writing, drawing”). See also prosopon.

senses: Someone who takes part in the sexual practice of fisting.
The act of disinterring.
An advocate of modernization.
A medical laboratory.
A Korean barbecued rib dish, usually made from beef
A translocon
To make (something) a crime; to make illegal under criminal law; to ban.
To treat as a criminal.
examples: Advocates for homeless people, the American Psychiatric Association and several left-leaning states, including New York, Illinois and Minnesota, argue that criminalizing homelessness only worsens the problem.
A group of homeless residents sued the city, challenging the ordinances and contending that the local laws essentially criminalized homelessness.

senses: Derived from salicin.
ety: From salicyl + -ic, from Latin salix (“willow tree”).

senses: To mark something with striations.
ety: From Latin striatum, past participle of strio (“to groove”).

senses: To make the crowing sound of a cock.
To crow in exultation.
ety: ] From Middle English Chauntecleer, from Old French Chantecler (modern French Chanteclair), the proper name of the cock in the literary cycle of Reynard the Fox, that also gave origin to chantecler, the name of a chicken breed; from chanter (“to sing, to crow”) + cler (“clear, clearly”). Attested in English since 1250–1300.

senses: a headsign; a destination sign: a moveable or electronic display mounted on a bus or other public transport vehicle to indicate its intended route and destination.
examples: When you arrive at the terminus, remember to change your desto.

senses: Synonym of forked.
examples: The forky lightning flashed, and the deep toned thunder reverberated peal on peal, while the shrieking winds rocked the tree tops, and poured their wild melody upon the ear.
At the sight of the young man it lashed its tail so violently that the earth trembled as if with an earthquake, while its forky tongue darted in and out with a deafening hissing noise.

senses: A monster preying upon human beings, who sucked the blood of children, often described as having the head and breasts of a woman and the lower half of a serpent.
ety: From Latin lamia, from Ancient Greek Λάμια (Lámia).

senses: A person who or a device which calls, summons loudly, or hails.
Prone to mumbling.
A breathing.
An aspirate.
Any spirituous preparation.
ety: Borrowed from Latin spīritus. Doublet of spirit, spirytus, sprite, spright, and esprit.

senses: To change, mutilate, or disfigure by cutting, tearing, rearranging, etc.
ety: From Middle English mangelen, manglen, from Anglo-Norman mangler, mahangler, frequentative of either Old French mangonner (“to cut to pieces”) or mahaigner (“to mutilate”), of Germanic origin, for which see mayhem. Alternate etymology derives mangle from Middle English *mankelen, a frequentative form of manken (“to mutilate”), from Old English *mancian, bemancian (“to maim”). More at mank.

senses: One of the three gunas in Hindu philosophy, representing things that are pure, divine, and spiritual.
That can be diffused.
The analysis of baseball, especially via its statistics.
ety: Coined by Bill James in 1980, from SABR (“Society for American Baseball Research”) + metrics.
examples: By the early 1990s it was clear that “sabermetrics,” the search for new baseball knowledge, was an activity that would take place mainly outside of baseball.

senses: An Asian plant, Solanum melongena, cultivated for its edible purple, green, or white ovoid fruit; eggplant.
The fruit of this plant, eaten as a vegetable.
A dark purple colour; eggplant.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French aubergine, from Catalan albergínia, from Arabic اَلْبَاذِنْجَان (al-bāḏinjān, “the aubergine”), from Classical Persian بَادِنْجَان (bādinjān), from بَاتِنْگَان (bātingān), from Sanskrit वातिङ्गण (vātiṅgaṇa, “the plant that cures the wind”), from Dravidian, ultimately from Proto-Dravidian *waẓVtV. Cognate with Malayalam വഴുതനങ്ങ (vaḻutanaṅṅa), Hindi बैंगन (baiṅgan). Doublet of brinjal, malidzano, and melongene.

senses: To cover or surface with tarmacadam.
